id: Neighbor: Miss Peach’s Body Didn’t Turn Out Right

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

But whose did? She’s crumpled where she’s supposed to be unfolded, something bad written on a piece of paper. Her walking is a devolution that hunches and shrinks everyone as she moves up the tree-lined street. I’m on my porch waving to my neighbors and having one of those honeyed afternoons when I don’t know who I am. I know everything else, though, and it’s ringing in my head. Then there she is in a pool on my front steps, laughing, asking about lunch, as if the bones of at least four different animals weren’t loose inside her, scurrying this way and that. Someone needs to find her a place to live, a hidey hole we can cram food in and get away from quickly. We could call her part bird and be done with it. But everyone is dying right under the surface these days, especially around the eyes. Death has crawled up into the face to nibble away whatever blocks its view of the stars. We’re riddled with it. It’s pulling our flesh into outrageous, unwilled positions, like the huge smile on my face as I lift her onto my lap and hold her together for a minute before I tell her she isn’t welcome here.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: But, She, Her

outputs.L1: But whose did? She is crumpled where she ought to be unfolded, like something terrible written on a piece of paper. Her walk is a devolution, hunching and shrinking everyone as she moves up the tree-lined street. I am on my porch, waving to my neighbors and drifting through one of those honeyed afternoons when I do not know who I am. I know everything else, though, and it is ringing in my head. Then there she is, pooled on my front steps, laughing, asking about lunch, as if the bones of at least four different animals were not loose inside her, scurrying this way and that. Someone needs to find her a place to live, some hidey-hole we can stuff with food and flee from quickly. We could call her part bird and be done with it. But everyone is dying just beneath the surface these days, especially around the eyes. Death has crawled up into the face to nibble away whatever blocks its view of the stars. We are riddled with it. It is pulling our flesh into outrageous, unwilled positions, like the enormous smile on my face as I lift her onto my lap and hold her together for a minute before I tell her she is not welcome here.
outputs.L2: But who did have one? She is collapsed in the places where she ought to open out, like a bad message scrawled onto a sheet of paper. The way she walks feels like a reversal of evolution, bending and diminishing everyone as she comes along the street lined with trees. I am standing on my porch, waving at the neighbors, in the middle of one of those syrupy afternoons when my own identity escapes me. Everything else, however, I understand, and it clangs inside my skull. Then suddenly she is there, gathered in a heap on my front steps, laughing and asking about lunch, as though the skeletons of no fewer than four separate animals are not rattling loose inside her, darting in every direction. Somebody ought to secure a place for her to stay, some little burrow where we can shove in food and retreat fast. We might simply decide she is partly bird and leave it at that. But these days everyone is perishing just beneath the skin, most noticeably around the eyes. Death has climbed into the face and begun gnawing away anything that keeps it from seeing the stars. It has tunneled through all of us. It drags our bodies into absurd poses we never chose, like the enormous grin stretched across my face as I pick her up, settle her in my lap, and keep her from coming apart for a moment before telling her she cannot stay here.
outputs.L3:
The narrator watches as a severely diminished and damaged woman approaches the house and collapses on the front steps. Her condition is immediately striking: she appears physically exhausted, emotionally broken, and almost emptied of ordinary human vitality. Despite this, she behaves with unsettling casualness, as if nothing unusual has happened. She asks about lunch in a familiar, everyday way, creating a sharp contrast between her outward manner and the visible evidence of suffering and deterioration.

In the narrator’s imagination, the woman becomes almost something less than human. She seems fragile, ruined, and difficult to look at directly, like a being who no longer belongs fully among the living. The narrator imagines that such a person should be hidden away somewhere, placed out of sight so that others do not have to confront her pain, weakness, or decay. This response reveals not only discomfort with the woman herself, but also a deeper fear of what she represents.

The passage suggests that death and decay are not separate from ordinary life, but are present beneath everyone’s surface. The woman’s damaged appearance makes visible something that usually remains hidden: the physical and emotional breakdown that all people carry within them. This sense of mortality is especially associated with faces and eyes, which reveal the truth of human vulnerability even when people try to conceal it.

Although the narrator briefly offers comfort to the woman, this compassion does not last. After a moment of tenderness or pity, the narrator ultimately tells her that she is not welcome. The scene therefore combines sympathy with rejection. The woman’s suffering is recognized, but it is also treated as something unbearable, something the narrator wants to push away rather than fully accept.
outputs.L4:
The passage presents a disturbing meditation on discomfort, mortality, and social rejection, using surreal and bodily imagery to expose what polite life usually tries to conceal. At its center is the narrator’s encounter with a damaged, unwelcome woman whose presence unsettles the people around her. She appears not simply as an individual in distress, but as a figure of physical and social breakdown: someone who carries visible signs of suffering, decay, and exclusion. Her body becomes a reminder of everything the surrounding world wants to deny—illness, aging, ugliness, dependence, and death.

The narrator’s response to her is conflicted. On one hand, there is fascination, pity, and even a momentary tenderness. The narrator seems to recognize the woman’s vulnerability and, for a brief time, feels drawn into an intimate awareness of her humanity. This tenderness matters because it breaks through the coldness of social convention. The woman is not merely an object of disgust or embarrassment; she is someone who suffers, and the narrator senses that suffering directly.

Yet this sympathy does not last in a simple or heroic way. The narrator is also repelled by the woman and participates, whether actively or passively, in her rejection. The passage shows how easily compassion can collapse under the pressure of discomfort and public judgment. The woman’s brokenness makes others uneasy because it reflects something universal. Her decay is not separate from them; it is an exaggerated version of what exists beneath everyone’s clean clothes, controlled manners, and respectable surfaces.

In this way, the passage suggests that death is not a distant event but a condition already present in living bodies. Decay permeates everyone, even those who appear healthy, proper, or socially acceptable. The grotesque imagery strips away illusion and reveals the shared physical fate that people try to hide. The woman becomes frightening not because she is entirely different, but because she makes visible what others are desperate to keep invisible.

The emotional force of the passage comes from this tension between recognition and rejection. The narrator briefly approaches the woman with a kind of intimate understanding, but ultimately she remains excluded. This makes the scene feel both tender and cruel. It acknowledges human connection while also showing the limits of that connection in a world governed by fear, disgust, and social boundaries. The woman’s presence exposes the fragility of compassion and the brutality of a society that rejects those who too openly display the truths of suffering, mortality, and bodily decline.
outputs.L5:
But she knew her story was not over.

She had faced doubts, delays, and difficult days, but her courage remained stronger than her fear. Every morning, she reminded herself that progress did not have to be perfect; it only had to be real. Her dreams were not always easy to follow, but they gave her a reason to keep moving forward.

But even when the path became uncertain, she trusted her heart. She learned from her mistakes, protected her peace, and chose hope again and again. Her strength was quiet, but it was powerful.

In the end, she discovered that her journey was not defined by what tried to stop her, but by the way she continued despite it all.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short piece of surreal literary horror in first person about a narrator seeing a deformed or broken woman arrive on their front steps during an idyllic neighborhood afternoon, ending with the narrator comforting her briefly before rejecting her.
counterfactuals.output:
The afternoon had been arranged like a display in a bakery window: lawns glazed with sun, sprinklers turning their silver wrists, children shrieking pleasantly around a blue plastic pool. Somewhere, someone was grilling peaches. The whole neighborhood smelled sugared and forgiven.

Then the woman came up my walk.

At first I thought she was carrying something heavy. Her body leaned around an invisible burden, one shoulder higher than the other, her knees bending the wrong way with each careful step. Her dress was the color of old flour and dragged behind her, wet at the hem though there had been no rain for weeks. When she reached the porch, I saw that her face had been assembled in a hurry: mouth too low, one eye clouded and shining near the cheek, hair pinned into the scalp with what looked like thorns.

The children across the street went quiet all at once.

She lifted a hand. It had too many knuckles.

“Please,” she said, and my name came out of her mouth in my mother’s voice.

I opened the door because I was raised to, because the sun was still bright, because the mailman was humming at the corner and nothing terrible could happen in such weather. Up close she smelled of pond water and warm pennies. She sank against me, trembling. For a moment I held her. Her bones shifted under my palms like furniture being moved in another room.

“It’s all right,” I whispered, though I knew it wasn’t. “You’re safe.”

She pressed her ruined face to my shoulder and began, softly, to purr.

Behind her, every house on the street had opened its front door. In each doorway stood the same woman, broken differently, waiting.

I eased her away. I smiled the way one smiles at a stray animal, with pity and a locked gate.

“No,” I said, and closed the door.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a flash fiction paragraph in a dark, uncanny style, with poetic grotesque imagery, about someone on a porch encountering a strange woman whose body seems wrong, mixing tenderness, revulsion, and social cruelty.
counterfactuals.output: On the porch, with the moths battering themselves to powder against the yellow bulb, I found her standing where the rain gutter wept—an old woman, or a girl worn inside out, her dress buttoned crooked over a body that did not seem to have agreed upon its own arrangement. One shoulder rose like a guilty hill, her elbows bent too many times beneath the sleeves, and when she smiled, tender as a torn lullaby, I saw the small dark glisten of her gums and felt, shamefully, both the urge to wrap her in my coat and the urge to lock the door. “They said you’d be kind,” she whispered, voice wet and careful, as if each word had to be lifted from a bowl of milk gone sour. Behind the curtains, my neighbors’ faces floated pale and eager, already sharpening the story of her ugliness into a weapon they could pass from mouth to mouth. She held out a hand—soft, warm, wrong—and I took it for one trembling second, long enough to feel the lonely animal inside her pressing against the cage of her skin, long enough to know that my pity was only another kind of looking away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a disturbing, lyrical prose vignette that begins with “But whose did?” and features a narrator describing a crumpled woman walking up a tree-lined street, asking about lunch, and being told she is not welcome.
counterfactuals.output:
But whose did? The question hung in the air like a torn sleeve on a branch, snagged and shivering, while the crumpled woman came up the tree-lined street with her coat folded wrong around her bones.

She moved as though she had been stored for years in a drawer too small for her, knees and elbows remembering corners. The trees leaned over her in their green, whispering way, making a tunnel of leaves and little trembling coins of light. Every step she took seemed to bring with it the faint dry sound of paper being crushed in a fist.

At the gate she paused.

“Is there lunch?” she asked.

Her voice was not hungry exactly. It was worse than hungry. It was careful. It had practiced not breaking.

Behind the screen door, someone breathed in, held it, then let it out in a shape colder than speech.

“You’re not welcome here.”

The woman nodded, as if this confirmed an appointment. As if she had come a long way to be denied in precisely those words. The trees kept shedding their flecks of sunlight onto her shoulders, dressing her briefly in gold, then taking it back.

She did not turn at once. She looked past the door, past the dim hallway, toward the place where a table might have been laid: white plates, dull knives, a glass sweating in its own small weather. Her mouth made the smallest motion, perhaps arranging an apology, perhaps tasting the ghost of soup.

Then she stepped away from the gate.

Down the street, the trees received her again, branch by branch, shadow by shadow, until she was only a crease moving through the afternoon, and then not even that.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a single dense paragraph of surreal fiction about alienation and mortality, where a person encounters a broken, birdlike woman on their porch and thinks about finding her a hiding place before sending her away.
counterfactuals.output: At dusk, when the neighborhood had already withdrawn its faces behind curtains and the sky looked bruised by some enormous thumb, I found her collapsed on my porch among the dead moths and unopened bills: a woman, or the ruin of one, with wrists thin as wishbones, clavicles sharp enough to tear the light, and a crooked fringe of dark feathers trembling along her shoulders as if a storm had nested there and died. She lifted her head when I opened the door, and her eyes were not pleading but anciently tired, the eyes of a migrating thing that had mistaken my house for a cliff, my welcome mat for a strip of shore. One wing—if it was a wing and not merely the memory of escape made flesh—dragged behind her, clicking softly against the boards, and in that sound I heard my own bones rehearsing their future, all the small hinges of my body preparing to fail. I thought of hiding her in the crawlspace beneath the stairs, among the jam jars and mouse poison, or in the cedar chest where my mother’s coat still held the shape of a vanished winter, or behind the furnace where dust grew in gray fur and no one, not even I, would look too closely; but every hiding place in my house was already occupied by something I had refused to mourn. She smelled of rain, rust, and hospital sheets, and when she opened her mouth a few white seeds spilled out instead of words, scattering over the porch like teeth. I wanted to ask who had done this to her, which sky had rejected her, whether there was a country where broken creatures were gathered and mended with golden thread, but I knew the answer would only be another form of hunger. So I stood there with my hand on the doorframe, feeling the old loneliness of being housed in a body that will one day evict me, and imagined wrapping her in blankets, tucking her beneath the floorboards, feeding her crumbs and secrets until spring; then I imagined the neighbors, the authorities, the slow contagion of pity, the way every rescued thing becomes a mirror. At last I knelt, brushed the moth dust from her cheek, and whispered directions to the abandoned church beyond the overpass, where the rafters were full of pigeons and the saints had no hands left to point or bless, and when she rose, shuddering, half-woman, half-bad omen, I turned away before she could thank or curse me, because I had already given her the only shelter I could bear to offer: the road away from me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
